title: The great chronicle
hookLine: the Mahavamsa, Sri Lanka's chronicle of kings and monks (Geiger, 1912)
carry: made for the serene joy of the faithful

lines: TOO LONG HERE, TOO SHORT THERE.
cards: The author opens by finding fault. An older telling of this history exists, he says in his first lines, but it is too long in some places, too short in others, and full of repetition.
So he will tell it again, in verse, free of those faults. That's how the Mahavamsa begins, Sri Lanka's chronicle of kings and monks, here in Wilhelm Geiger's English translation.
Tradition names its author as a monk called Mahanama.

teach.b: First, how it begins. Before a single king, the chronicle brings the Buddha to the island.

Its first chapter tells of three visits: one to drive out the yakkhas, spirits who held the land; one to settle a quarrel between two serpent kings fighting over a jeweled throne; and one to Kelaniya, at a serpent king's invitation.
Before the history starts, the chronicle lays a blessing on the land.

teach.h: KINGS AND MONKS, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: Second, what it covers: kings and monks, side by side. Who built which stupa, who brought which relic, who supported the monasteries and who neglected them. It judges kings partly by how they treated the teaching.
Third, what it says it is for.

teach.h: WRITTEN FOR THE JOY OF THE FAITHFUL.
teach.b: Its chapters close by naming their purpose: the work was made for the serene joy and the stirring of the faithful. The book tells you plainly it isn't neutral. It is history written to move its readers.
Fourth, how it is read now. Historians use it with care, checking it against inscriptions and ruins; they find it valuable and also shaped by its aims.
Buddhists in Sri Lanka read it as the story of how the teaching came to their island and was kept there. Some of its war stories are read in very different ways by different readers today.

teach.h: READ WITH LOVE AND WITH CARE.
teach.b: A chronicle like this is a community telling its own story, with love and with a point of view.
Knowing both is part of reading it well.

how: In Sri Lanka the Mahavamsa is read in schools and monasteries and retold at temples and festivals as the story of how the teaching came to the island, while historians study it alongside inscriptions and archaeology.

a list of the Buddha's past lives in verse
the island's oldest law code for its kings

games.q: the great chronicle: tap the pairs.
p: the monk tradition names as author

games.q: you're writing the history of your island's faith. where do you begin?
o: with the first king who ruled.
with the Buddha himself visiting the island.
games.why: the Mahavamsa begins with the Buddha's visits to the island, laying a blessing on the land before the history of kings starts.

practice: Bring to mind the place where you live, or where you grew up, and the story it tells about itself: a founding, a flood, a hero, a name on a street sign.
Notice what the story wants you to feel, and what it might leave out, with no judgment, just breathing.
